detail: supported
Does not address view-dependent phase function artifacts [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that the evidence does not address view-dependent phase function artifacts. The provided text from Source [S1] explicitly confirms this in the passage: 'However, this work does not explore how volumetric TAA is affected by highly view dependent phase functions due to scope.' This directly supports the claim that the issue is not addressed.
supported
# Acquire per-frame sub-froxel jitter offset from pre-defined set [S1, unofficial]

The claim states that a per-frame sub-froxel jitter offset is acquired from a pre-defined set. The evidence explicitly confirms this in multiple passages: 'A per-frame sub-froxel jitter offset is acquired from a pre-defined set of points' and 'For froxels that can be reprojected, acquire a sub-froxel jitter offset from a pre-calculated list containing the Halton(2,3,5) sequence of length 16.' The evidence also notes that 'Each froxel uses the same per-frame offset,' which aligns with the claim's implication of a shared pre-defined set for the frame.
supported
- **Reprojection Vector:** A vector describing camera translation and rotation between frames [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that the Reprojection Vector describes camera translation and rotation between frames. The evidence in Source [S1] explicitly states: '...eprojection vector that describes how the camera was moved and rotated from the previous frame into the current one.' It further clarifies that 'the vector only contains information about how the camera moved in between frames' and 'does not describe any movement of the froxel itself'. This aligns perfectly with the claim.
supported
# Apply jitter offset only to the z-axis, remaining centered in x and y [S1, unofficial]

The claim states that the jitter offset is applied only to the z-axis, remaining centered in x and y. Source [S1] explicitly supports this in multiple passages: 1) 'If depth-only jittering is used, apply the jitter offset only to the z-axis, remaining centered in the x and y directions.' 2) 'By instead centering the sampling point in the middle of the froxel and offsetting it only along the froxel's depth (in the camera forward direction)...' 3) 'If depth-only jittering is used, the jitter offset is applied only to the z-axis, remaining centered in the x and y directions.' The claim accurately reflects the specific 'depth-only' or 'z-axis only' jittering strategy described in the evidence.
supported
# Center the sampling point in the middle of the froxel, then offset only along depth [S1, unofficial]

The evidence explicitly states that to reduce spatial complexity and improve temporal stability, one should 'center the sampling point in the middle of the froxel and offset it only along the froxel's depth (in the camera forward direction).' It further notes that this specific approach is used in Frostbite.
supported
Apply the jitter offset to the sampling position within the froxel [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that the jitter offset is applied to the sampling position within the froxel. Source [S1] explicitly confirms this in multiple passages: 'Apply the jitter offset to the sampling position within the froxel during the compute shader evaluation of in-scattered radiance' and 'At the jittered sample position, the participating media density and in-scattered lighting are evaluated.' The evidence fully supports the claim.
supported
This technique is used in the Frostbite engine [S1, unofficial].

The evidence explicitly states in Source [S1] passages: 'This is the approach used in Frostbite [3].' This directly supports the claim that the technique (specifically the 1D jittering strategy along the froxel's depth) is used in the Frostbite engine.
supported

Sub-Froxel Temporal Jittering is a technique for real-time volumetric rendering that offsets the sampling position within a froxel along the camera's depth axis to enable temporal supersampling and anti-aliasing [S1, unofficial].

The evidence explicitly states that sub-froxel temporal jittering is a technique used in real-time volumetric rendering (specifically mentioning Frostbite and Godot pipelines). It confirms that the technique involves offsetting the sampling position within a froxel along the camera's depth axis (z-axis) to reduce spatial complexity and improve temporal stability. Furthermore, the evidence links this process to temporal supersampling and anti-aliasing by accumulating new information about participating media over time.
supported
It is constant for all froxels in a frame, as froxels represent static world-space positions [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that the jitter offset is constant for all froxels in a frame because froxels represent static world-space positions. The evidence supports this in two ways: 1) It explicitly states that 'each froxel uses the same per-frame offset' and 'each froxel having the same per-frame offset,' confirming the constant nature across froxels. 2) It explains that the reprojection vector (used to handle the static world-space positions) 'does not describe any movement of the froxel itself, as the world-space position it represents is not associated with any movement,' confirming the static nature of the positions.
supported

It distinguishes itself from full 3D jittering by restricting movement to the z-axis, thereby reducing spatial variance in the x and y directions to improve temporal stability when accumulating history [S1, unofficial].

The evidence explicitly states that some implementations 'only jitter the sampling point along the z-axis (depth) of the froxel' and that this approach involves 'offsetting it only along the froxel's depth... remaining centered in the x and y directions.' It further explains that this is done because 'sampling across the entirety of the froxel... introduces signal variance in the x and y directions' and that restricting jitter to one dimension (depth/z-axis) 'reduces this spatial complexity' to 'improve temporal stability.' This aligns perfectly with the claim.
supported
Commonly uses Halton(2,3) of length 8 or 16, or Halton(2,3,5) of length 16 [S1, unofficial].

The evidence explicitly states that 'Low-discrepancy sequences like Halton(2,3) of length 8 or 16 are commonly used' and that for reprojection-capable froxels, a 'pre-calculated list containing the Halton(2,3,5) sequence of length 16' is used. All specific details in the claim are present in the source text.
supported
The jitter offset is pre-calculated and passed as a shader parameter, requiring no additional per-froxel computation beyond the offset addition [S1, unofficial].

The evidence explicitly states in Source [S1] passages that 'A per-frame sub-froxel jitter offset is acquired from a pre-defined set of points... This allows the jitter offset to be pre-calculated and passed to the GPU as a shader parameter.' It further confirms that the offset is applied during the compute shader evaluation, implying that the computation within the shader is limited to adding this offset to the sampling position, with no additional complex per-froxel calculation required for the jitter generation itself.
supported
It was adapted for froxel-based rendering to provide temporal anti-aliasing for in-scattered radiance, building on the concept of temporal supersampling [S1, unofficial].

The evidence explicitly states that the method involves offsetting the sampling point from the center of the froxel each frame (sub-froxel jittering) to learn and accumulate new information, which acts as temporal anti-aliasing. It confirms this builds on the concept of temporal supersampling. The evidence also details that this approach (specifically 1D jittering along the depth axis) is used in Frostbite and is part of a froxel-based rendering pipeline for in-scattered radiance.
supported
# If reprojection fails, no sub-froxel temporal jittering is applied [S1, unofficial]

The claim states that if reprojection fails, no sub-froxel temporal jittering is applied. The evidence in Source [S1] explicitly confirms this in the section describing the shader passes: 'If reprojection fails, i.e. if the reprojection vector points outside of the history buffer, no sub-froxel temporal jittering is applied, as jittering is only useful when current frame samples can be blended with the history [4].' This matches the claim exactly.
supported
- Sequence Length: 8 or 16 [S1, unofficial].

The evidence explicitly states in multiple passages that 'A low-discrepancy sequence such as the Halton(2,3) sequence of length 8 or 16 is commonly used' and that 'The Halton sequence can be extended into three dimensions'. It also mentions specific implementations using sequences of length 16 (e.g., Halton(2,3,5) of length 16). Thus, the claim that the sequence length is 8 or 16 is fully supported by the text.
